interactions.label: A 55-year-old man presents with left ear pain and a normal otoscopic examination

params.question: A 55-year-old man presents with left ear pain and a normal otoscopic examination. He also reports progressive hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Through which nerve pathway is the otalgia most likely referred?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The auriculotemporal nerve mediates referred pain from dental pathology and temporomandibular joint dysfunction, not from laryngeal or hypopharyngeal sources.

answers.text: Arnold's nerve — auricular branch of the vagus (CN X)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arnold's nerve connects the posterior ear canal to the larynx and hypopharynx. Hoarseness and dysphagia with a normal ear exam strongly suggest a laryngeal or hypopharyngeal carcinoma referring pain through this pathway.

answers.text: Jacobson's nerve — tympanic branch of CN IX

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Jacobson's nerve shares sensory territory with the tonsil and oropharynx; it would not explain hoarseness, which localises to the larynx.
The great auricular nerve mediates referred pain from cervical spondylosis, typically presenting with neck stiffness rather than hoarseness and dysphagia.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is Arnold's nerve (CN X). Hoarseness and dysphagia point to a laryngeal or hypopharyngeal source, and Arnold's nerve is the pathway that refers pain from these structures to the ear.
Correct. Arnold's nerve (CN X) is the pathway linking the ear to the larynx and hypopharynx — the key pathway to remember when ear pain presents with voice change or swallowing difficulty.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old patient presents with persistent unilateral ear pain for six weeks

params.question: A 62-year-old patient presents with persistent unilateral ear pain for six weeks. Otoscopy is normal, the oral cavity and oropharynx show no lesions, the TMJ is non-tender, and there are no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Which step in the otalgia workup should be performed next?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT temporal bone is indicated when middle-ear pathology such as cholesteatoma is suspected. With a normal otoscopic exam, the priority is to exclude a referred cause by visualising the aerodigestive tract.

answers.text: Prescribe analgesics and review in four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Watchful waiting is dangerous here. In an adult with persistent unilateral otalgia and a normal ear, a head-and-neck malignancy must be excluded before attributing the pain to a benign cause.

This is the most commonly omitted yet most critical step. It directly visualises the nasopharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx — sites where carcinomas can present with referred otalgia before causing any local symptoms.
Audiometry assesses hearing but does not identify the source of referred otalgia. The next priority is direct visualisation of the upper aerodigestive tract.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is indirect laryngoscopy (fibreoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy). With otoscopy, oral cavity, TMJ, and neck examination all normal, the last step — and the one most often omitted — is direct visualisation of the larynx and pharynx.

Correct. Indirect laryngoscopy is the step most often skipped — yet it is the only way to directly visualise the nasopharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx, where occult carcinomas can present solely as ear pain.

interactions.label: In perichondritis of the pinna, the lobule is characteristically spared because

params.question: In perichondritis of the pinna, the lobule is characteristically spared because it contains no cartilage and therefore no perichondrium.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. The lobule lacks cartilage entirely; it is made of fibrous tissue and fat. Without cartilage, there is no perichondrium to become infected — which is precisely why lobule-sparing is the pathognomonic sign of perichondritis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The lobule is composed of fibrous tissue and fat without any cartilage. Since perichondritis is infection of the perichondrium — the membrane investing cartilage — the lobule is anatomically incapable of being involved. Lobule-sparing is the defining clinical clue.

params.question: A 70-year-old diabetic man has severe left ear pain that has worsened despite two weeks of topical antibiotic drops. Otoscopy reveals granulation tissue at the floor of the bony-cartilaginous junction. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and review in one week

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amoxicillin does not cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the causative organism, and oral antibiotics are inadequate for skull base osteomyelitis. This presentation demands parenteral anti-pseudomonal therapy.

answers.text: Perform aural toilet and switch to topical clotrimazole

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clotrimazole is for otomycosis (fungal infection), which presents with itching and dark or white debris — not granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction in a diabetic.

answers.text: Assess facial nerve function, order a technetium-99 bone scan, and start intravenous anti-pseudomonal antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction in a diabetic is pathognomonic for malignant otitis externa. Facial nerve testing detects early skull base involvement, the Tc-99 scan maps disease extent, and 6–8 weeks of IV antibiotics are required alongside strict glycaemic control.

answers.text: Continue the same topical drops for another two weeks and add oral prednisolone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Continuing topical therapy alone delays diagnosis of skull base osteomyelitis. Systemic steroids would further immunocompromise a diabetic patient with an aggressive Pseudomonas infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is facial nerve assessment, Tc-99 bone scan, and IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics. This presentation — a diabetic with granulation tissue at the canal floor unresponsive to topical treatment — is malignant otitis externa, a skull base osteomyelitis requiring aggressive intervention.

Correct. In a diabetic with intractable ear pain and granulation at the bony-cartilaginous junction, malignant otitis externa is the diagnosis until proven otherwise — requiring urgent facial nerve assessment, imaging, and IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics.

interactions.label: A 16-year-old presents with foul-smelling ear discharge and pearly white debris

params.question: A 16-year-old presents with foul-smelling ear discharge and pearly white debris visible in the attic region. The perforation involves the pars flaccida. Which combination of features most reliably classifies this as unsafe (atticoantral) disease rather than safe (tubotympanic) disease?

answers.text: Duration of discharge exceeding six months and bilateral involvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Duration and laterality do not reliably distinguish tubotympanic from atticoantral disease. Both types can be chronic and bilateral.

answers.text: Marginal or attic perforation with foul, cheesy discharge indicating keratin accumulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The safe–unsafe distinction rests on two features: perforation site (central pars tensa = safe; attic or marginal = unsafe) and discharge character (mucoid = mucosal disease; foul cheesy debris = squamous epithelium trapping keratin, i.e. cholesteatoma). A pars flaccida perforation with keratin debris confirms atticoantral disease requiring surgery.

answers.text: Presence of conductive hearing loss greater than 30 dB

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both tubotympanic and atticoantral disease cause conductive hearing loss. The degree of loss does not reliably distinguish between them.

answers.text: Failure to respond to topical antibiotic ear drops within two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Treatment response is not a reliable distinguishing criterion. Waiting for treatment failure in atticoantral disease risks progressive bone erosion and complications such as facial palsy or intracranial abscess.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is marginal or attic perforation with foul, cheesy discharge. Tubotympanic (safe) disease has a central pars tensa perforation with mucoid discharge; atticoantral (unsafe) disease has an attic or marginal perforation with keratin debris — this is cholesteatoma, which erodes bone and requires surgery.

Correct. The perforation site and discharge character are the two pillars of the safe–unsafe distinction. Attic or marginal perforation with foul cheesy debris means cholesteatoma — mandatory surgical management.
